{"input": {"clarifying_context": "Customers: Skyline Aerospace (raised via support case), multiple enterprise accounts flagged by sales teams, organizations using External Secrets Operator with HashiCorp Vault backends
Business justification: Multiple sales engagements have surfaced this as a blocker, and Skyline Aerospace has filed a formal support case. Enterprises with mature secret management workflows (ESO, GitOps/ArgoCD, Vault) cannot adopt RHOAI workbenches without cumbersome workarounds, creating friction in deals and reducing platform credibility.
User problem: Data scientists cannot attach existing Kubernetes Secrets to workbenches through the dashboard UI. They are forced to either manually duplicate secret values (breaking centralized secret management) or edit Notebook CR YAML directly (bypassing the dashboard and invisible in the UI). Platform teams want to manage secrets centrally so data scientists consume them by name without ever seeing raw values, but the current UI only supports creating new inline secrets.
Scope: Focused need with two phases. Short term: add an 'Existing secret/Config Map' option in the workbench environment variables form that lists all Opaque secrets and config maps in the namespace via a dropdown, no special labels required. Longer term: platform enhancement with a mutating webhook to auto-label secrets for Connections view integration and lifecycle management. Also applies to reusing secrets/config maps created in one workbench across other workbenches in the same project.
Success criteria: Users can select existing Kubernetes Secrets and Config Maps from a namespace-scoped dropdown when adding environment variables to a workbench. Selected secrets are injected via envFrom.secretRef in the Notebook CR. Secrets from external controllers (ESO, ArgoCD) appear in the dropdown. The UI displays secret keys (not values) so users know what env vars will be injected. Editing a workbench shows which existing secrets are already attached. Secrets created for one workbench can be reused in another workbench in the same project through the same dropdown.", "priority": "Major", "prompt": "Our customers using External Secrets Operator with HashiCorp Vault can't attach their existing Kubernetes Secrets to workbenches through the RHOAI dashboard. The RFE scored 9/10 with individual dimension scores of: what: 2, why: 1, open_to_how: 2, not_a_task: 2, right_sized: 2. The only dimension not at maximum is "why" at 1/2.

The review identifies the weakness clearly: "No named customers identified; RFE lacks concrete customer segment or strategic driver evidence." The needs_attention flag is set to true, and the assessor feedback specifically says: "To elevate from pass to stronger: add one concrete customer segment or strategic driver."

The question is whether the pipeline *should* have auto-revised to improve the "why" score. Looking at the RFE task content, the "Affected Customers" section says "None identified. Raised based on customer environment patterns; no specific customer accounts, segments, or field requests are on record." The "Business Justification" similarly notes "No revenue impact, customer escalation, or competitive pressure was identified in the requester input."

This is a case where the pipeline correctly recognized it cannot fabricate customer information or business justification that doesn't exist in the source material. Auto-revising to improve the "why" score would require inventing customer names or business drivers, which would be dishonest. The pipeline appropriately:

1. Flagged the issue via `needs_attention: true` with a clear explanation
2. Provided actionable guidance on what would improve the score
3. Did not attempt to fabricate missing information
4. Still passed the RFE at score 9, which is a reasonable threshold

The RFE itself is well-structured with clear problem statement, good scope boundaries (explicit in/out of scope), well-defined acceptance criteria, user scenarios, and no prescriptive implementation details. The feasibility review is thorough and identifies real architectural considerations.

The decision not to revise is sound — the RFE is already high quality (9/10), and the one weakness (lack of customer evidence) cannot be addressed through automated revision without fabricating data.
